new_statements.quote: 2.1.3. Tone. The Mambiloid languages are register tone languages, all appearing to have either three or four tones at the lexical level. [...] The different tones, at least in most Mambiloid languages also combine on one syllable to form a number of tone contours. Tone also operates grammatically in Mambiloid languages, with modifications in the tone of the verb indicating, among other functions, imperative mood and changes in tense.

new_statements.relation_note: Register tone, 3-4 levels, contour combinations, grammatical tone; vowel systems with high back/central unrounded vowel; palatal obstruents and prenasalized C1; labialization; no stress discussion.
new_statements.rule_in_words: All Mambiloid languages (Ndunda enumerated among them) are register tone languages with three or four lexical tone levels; tones may combine into contours on one syllable; tone also marks grammatical categories on the verb. Nothing is said about stress or accent anywhere in the chapter.
new_statements.exceptions: Author's own caveat (p. 84): 'It must be emphasized that the vast majority of these languages have not been studied at all, and that proper investigation may result in substantial modification of these generalizations.' Number of tones for Ndunda specifically is not given (three vs four unresolved).
new_statements.identity_note: Family overview of Mambiloid written after the Jan 1999 Blench & Connell trip: Table One 'Member languages of the Mambiloid group' lists 'Ndunda (300)' beside 'Kamkam/Mvanip (100)', so Ndunda [nuh] is explicitly within the scope of the chapter's generalizations; the author co-collected the only Ndunda wordlist. The tone statement itself is about 'the Mambiloid languages' as a group, not about Ndunda individually, and the illustrative systems are Ba-Mambila and Sundani-Kwanja. | One-page conference abstract by the co-collector of the only Ndunda wordlist; it enumerates 'Tep, Mbongo Mvanip, Ndunda, Somyev, and Nizaa' among the c. 10 Mambiloid languages and then generalizes over 'most Mambiloid languages'. Ndunda [nuh] is therefore inside the scope of the tone statement, but no Ndunda-specific tone count is given and the underlying Ndunda data are an unpublished extended wordlist. The file was placed held by the project by another compiler (W3) after A finished;7 MB PDF and kept the extract.

new_statements.quote: The Bantoid sub-group Mambiloid comprises some 10 different languages of which Mambila. with at least 12 different dialects and over 100,000 speakers, is the largest; among the others are Kwanja, Ndoro, Vute, and Wawa, each of which also has dialectal variation, and Tep, Mbongo Mvanip, Ndunda, Somyev, and Nizaa, none of which is reported to have demonstrable dialectal variation. While for many of these the only data available are extended wordlists, most Mambiloid languages appear to have four contrastive lexical tones; Nizaa and Vute have three lexical tones, while one distinguishing feature among Mambila lects is three as opposed to four tones.

new_statements.relation_note: Most Mambiloid languages (Ndunda listed) have four contrastive lexical tones; 4-tone systems not in correspondence across languages, hence independent developments; proposes Proto-Mambiloid tone reconstruction. No stress statement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ndunda is enumerated among the Mambiloid languages, most of which 'appear to have four contrastive lexical tones' (Nizaa and Vute three; Mambila lects three or four); the four-tone systems are said to have evolved independently. Nothing on stress or accent. Group-level statement resting, for Ndunda, on an unpublished extended wordlist.
